data.name: Life of a Wizard
data.detailed_description:
Write an archmage's autobiography in this 80-year 130,000-word interactive fiction! Play good or evil, man or woman, as you bring peace to the kingdom or take over the world with your sorcery. Brew potions, raise the dead, summon mythical beasts, control men's minds, and blast away your enemies.

Life of a Wizard is an epic interactive novel where you control the main character. In each chapter, your choices determine how the story proceeds.

Will you find romance, get married, or have children? Will you become the arch-mage, grand bishop, nature-loving druid, hardened battle-mage or even an undead lich? The choice is yours!

reviews.review:
Reviewing (mostly) every game (or DLC) in my library, part 647:

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️☆☆☆☆ (6/10)

I always feel a little bit bad about reviewing Mike Walter's games. They are fun, wide, and surprisingly immersive! Would I call them "good," though? Ehhhhh. Maybe, maybe not. Walter has a clear [i]modus operandi[/i], where he'll whip up a banger of a stat and mechanic system, toss in some lighthearted tropes, and add multiple branches to explore. However, the big cons I am obligated to point out are (1) the short lengths of his works, (2) workmanlike prose, and (3) lack of character ... anything. You need to know what you're getting into with Walter's games—and I emphasize them as [i]games, [/i]not as books, like some of the other text-based games are. Still, despite my complaints, I can always count on Walter for an hour or two of fun. [b]Once again, big thanks to the staff for the review copy![/b]

[b][h2]Pros:[/h2][/b]
✅ [b]A staggering amount of character customization.[/b] Nine schools of magic, numerous knowledge skills, multiple races, factions, equipment, companions, and countless character builds mean your wizard can feel completely different from one playthrough to the next. Few Hosted Games offer this much mechanical freedom.

✅ [b]Fantastic replay value.[/b] This is easily the game's biggest strength. You'll never come close to seeing everything in a single playthrough. Different builds, skills, and decisions lock entire questlines, endings, achievements, and major story branches behind them. Thankfully, a complete run takes only about an hour or two (and even less once you know what you're doing), so experimentation is painless. Like, what do you mean I can have a child? And raise my child to become the Royal Wizard after me, or place them on the throne? Or for myself, I could choose to be an Archdruid or Archbishop or Archmage? 

✅ [b]Great power fantasy![/b] There's a constant stream of action going on. You start as an ordinary child in a quiet village, then attend a magical academy, assemble an adventuring party, slay monsters, explore ancient ruins, shape the fate of kingdoms, and eventually become one of the most influential people in the world. The story itself follows a fairly traditional "save the kingdom" fantasy structure, but that's not really the point. The fun comes from the countless adventures you get to go on. I also liked the end-game kingdom-building.

[b][h2]Mixed:[/h2][/b]
🟨 [b]The stat system can encourage optimization over roleplaying.[/b] The game has a noticeable "rich get richer" problem. High Illusion checks often reward more Illusion. High Conjuration rewards more Conjuration. Figuring out how to min-max can be rewarding, however. In RPGs, I usually focus on a single specialty, but that's not the way to go for Walter's games. [i]Life of a Wizard[/i] [i]heavily[/i] rewards diversification due to the low stat caps, easy way to build stats, and multiple stat checks.

[b][h2]Cons:[/h2][/b]
🟥 [b]The characters are little more than names on a stat sheet.[/b] This is by far my biggest criticism. Friends, companions, romances—even your own family—get so little development that it's hard to attach to anyone. They're functional, but rarely memorable. Your family dies when you're sixty? They get one page of mourning. RIP. But hey, at least I got 200 Gold from them! Bye bye, Mom and Dad! Gun to my head, if you asked me to tell the difference between my adventuring party, I couldn't. All the characters you meet, even the love interests and villains, are flatter than a pancake. They have their one (1) defined role, and that's it. Character interactions themselves are limited. I don't think I ever conversed with my Cleric or Thief? Eh, whatever. They killed who I told them to!

🟥 [b]The pacing is relentless.[/b] Living an entire lifetime in roughly an hour means almost every event ends just as it begins. One moment you're enrolling in the academy, the next you're slaying dragons, leading kingdoms, growing grey, and watching decades pass. You journey from region to region in the blink of an eye, and the aftermath of killing a dragon is explained in just a few minutes of reading. You go through 80 years of your life in an hour, and the pacing reflects it.

🟥 [b]Walter's prose.[/b] I don't quite know how to say this politely, but his prose is a tad on the bland side. It's, ah, the literary equivalent of a well-worn pair of boots: plain, dependable, and built to get you where you're going. And that's all. The setting is your typical generic fantasy setting, and it relies on a lot of "telling" instead of "showing." There's a lot of "you feel sad," "you feel pleased," or even "this new king is weak and timid, so therefore he sucks!"

[hr]
If you enjoyed this review, please check out my curator page to find more: [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/45814768-Verdict-Play-or-Pass/]Verdict: Play or Pass.[/url] Also, please leave a like and visit [url=https://steamcommunity.com/groups/Indie_Gems]IndieGems[/url] and our [url=https://www.youtube.com/@IndieGems2]YouTube channel[/url] for more reviews like this one.
